response.explanation: authorize() only checks the password when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch (line 131) is chosen on `credentials.backupCode`, and it never looks at `totpCode`. A request that sends `backupCode` together with any non-empty `totpCode`, such as "000000", skips the password check. The `identityProvider !== CAL && !totpCode` guards are skipped in the same way. The backup-code branch never validates `totpCode`, so the junk value is never rejected. The only remaining factor is the backup code, so a stolen or guessed backup code alone is enough to sign in. The login UI clears `totpCode` before sending a backup code, but the server does not enforce this. The skip was meant for the external TOTP flow that has already authenticated, and the new branch inherits it.

response.consequence: A single-use 2FA backup code can be replayed in parallel requests. The impact is limited because the attacker must already know the password and a valid code.
response.explanation: In authorize, the encrypted backupCodes blob is read in the earlier findUnique. It is decrypted and checked with indexOf. The matching slot is then nulled and the whole blob is written back with prisma.user.update, keyed only on id. There is no transaction and no compare-and-swap on the stored blob. Two concurrent logins with the same valid code and password both read the blob before either write lands. Both pass indexOf and both succeed. The concurrent writes can also overwrite each other, so a second code used in parallel can be restored. Login guessing is rate-limited: checkRateLimitAndThrowError runs on each authorize call with the user's email. disable.ts has no limiter, but it requires an authenticated session and the password for CAL users.
response.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so a single-use code can be accepted twice

response.explanation: The identity-provider checks and the password check in authorize (lines 113-129) all depend on `!credentials.totpCode`. A request with a victim's email and any non-empty totpCode, with no password, skips all three. If the user has twoFactorEnabled=false, neither the backup-code branch (line 131) nor the TOTP branch (line 157) runs. Nothing later verifies the password or rejects a totpCode when 2FA is off. Line 205 then returns the user object, which means the sign-in succeeds. The same holds for users with a non-CAL identity provider. If 2FA is enabled, the password is still skipped, so a valid TOTP alone is enough to log in. The backup-code branch added by this change has the same problem: totpCode plus backupCode skips the password check.
